title: Swarm Benchmarking & KV-caching Regression Playbook
content:
Purpose:
This note documents a lightweight, repeatable approach for finding regressions that affect KV cache behavior, kernel scheduling interactions, and tail latency in the serving runtime. The approach centers around a "swarm" harness: many small, diverse synthetic clients that interleave requests to exercise scheduling, eviction, and kernel warmup paths concurrently (closer to real multi-tenant traffic than single-user microbenchmarks).

Scope and intent:
- Focus: KV cache miss/hit patterns, eviction storms, kernel launch costs under scheduling churn, and regression detection heuristics.
- Not intended to replace microbench isolates (we still run those), but to complement them with a multi-stream concurrency stress harness that surfaces cross-cutting regressions.
- This is a playbook for triage: how to run the swarm, what to collect, and how to interpret signals.

High-level goals:
1) Surface regressions that only appear when multiple interactive sequences share the same model instance (KV state + scheduler interplay).
2) Provide reproducible traces and minimal repros (golden workload) for engineering and perf triage.
3) Keep harness low-friction so product teams can run it in CI or on-demand.

Harness design (swarm-runner):
- Orchestrator spawns N worker clients (N configurable, default 64) that run short sessions (5–50 tokens each) with deterministic random seeds.
- Workload mix: prefix-heavy (70%), long-tail queries (20% 200–1000 tokens), and embeddings/aux ops (10%) to emulate auxiliary load.
- Interleave timing: poisson-arrival with configurable mean to simulate burstiness; supports scheduled bursts to create eviction storms.
- Workers reuse shared model endpoint(s) to force KV reuse/eviction across clients; supports dedicated vs shared instance modes to pinpoint routing policy effects.

Key metrics to collect (per-request and aggregated):
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 generation time, and per-token latency breakdown (first token vs streaming tokens).
- KV cache: per-request KV hits, misses, eviction events, and cache occupancy over time. Track hit rate by token position (prefix vs continuation).
- Kernel telemetry: kernel launch count per request, average kernel duration, and top-3 kernels by total time.
- GPU metrics: SM occupancy, memory alloc/free spikes, PCIe transfers (for offload tests), and % time spent in kernels vs scheduling overhead.
- Scheduler metrics: preemption events, queue depth, time-in-queue per request slice.
- Error/degenerate signals: token drops, OOMs, retries/fallbacks, fallback model invocations.

Tracing strategy and sampling:
- Two-tier tracing to limit overhead: lightweight sampling (1% of requests) with headers and event markers, and targeted full traces for failing windows.
- Lightweight trace payload: request id, seed, KV hit count, kernel count, GPU time, and a short stack of scheduling events. Collected continuously.
- Full trace capture: when a sliding window of metric anomalies (p99 > baseline*1.3 or KV miss rate spike > +10% in 30s) occurs, enable verbose tracing for N seconds (default 60s) and export full CUDA kernel traces + KV cache timeline.
- Correlate traces with wall-clock and GPU clock via synchronized monotonic timestamps.

Repro strategy (golden workload):
- When swarm detects a regression, it attempts to localize: reduce concurrency, switch to dedicated-mode, and replay the same deterministic seed set on a single instance to see if regression reproduces in isolation.
- If isolated repro fails, escalate to golden-workload: a 2-min canonical stream of 256 deterministic sessions that mirror the failing request mix; this is used for PR-level regression checks.

Regression detection heuristics and alerts:
- Metric-based thresholds: configurable per-model baseline. Default alert if p99 latency increases by >20% AND p50 increases by >5% over baseline for 5m.
- Composite signal: combine p99 spike, KV miss-rate delta, and kernel-launch-rate change. A high-confidence regression requires at least two of three signals crossing thresholds.
- Persistent vs transient: transient spikes that resolve within 2m are marked as "flaky" and logged for observability; persistent anomalies trigger CI regressions and a triage ticket.

Microbench complement tests (quick recipes):
- Single-stream long-context run: replay a 2k-token single-session to stress KV retention and measure per-position KV hit curve.
- Cold-start kernel shot: launch X short requests to measure first-token kernel overhead across model variants/quantization configs.
- Eviction storm: ramp concurrency to saturate KV capacity and measure eviction-induced latency tail.
- Kernel-schedule competition: co-locate a heavy batching job with low-latency interactive streams and measure interference.

Example quick commands (harness CLI snippets):
- run swarm: ./swarm-runner -n 64 -mean-arrival-ms 50 -burst 200 -mode shared -seed-file samples/golden-seeds.json
- collect light traces: ./swarm-runner --trace-sample 0.01 --outdir /tmp/swarmlogs
- trigger full capture on anomaly: ./swarm-runner --auto-capture --capture-duration 60

Interpreting results (common patterns and next steps):
- Pattern: p99 jumps with KV miss-rate spikes and concurrent kernel-launch-rate increase => likely eviction contention. Next steps: increase KV capacity for test, reproduce with dedicated instance, collect full trace and inspect eviction timeline.
- Pattern: tail latency increases but KV hit-rate stable, GPU kernel duration increases => kernel code regression or new kernel path. Next steps: run kernel microbench for top kernels and diff kernel timings between baseline and suspect build.
- Pattern: sporadic large latencies correlated with scheduler preemptions => scheduler priorities/timeslice changes. Next steps: capture scheduler event timeline and test with altered scheduling config.

Low-friction CI integration suggestions:
- Add a nightly "swarm-smoke" job that runs with N=16 and the golden workload; fail build if composite-regression-detection fires.
- Add a PR gate that runs a tiny golden-workload sample (N=4, 30s) for changes touching scheduler, KV logic, or kernel dispatch.

Data retention and privacy notes:
- Traces may include customer request tokens in test harnesses; default to synthetic seeds and scrub any real user data.
- Keep full traces for 30 days, lightweight metrics for 90 days.

Playbook for an incident (short):
1) Confirm baseline and collect lightweight traces for the interval.
2) Run dedicated golden-workload replay; if reproducible, capture full CUDA traces.
3) Pin suspect commit(s), run microbench kernel isolates, and check for kernel-duration deltas.
4) If KV eviction implicated, increase cache size and rerun; if mitigated, plan config change or code fix.
5) Create triage ticket with attached traces, microbench results, and suggested mitigation (config or revert).

Checklist (quick):
- [ ] Run swarm with same model binary as prod
- [ ] Collect lightweight traces continuously
- [ ] Configure auto-capture thresholds
- [ ] Save deterministic seeds for repro
- [ ] Run microbench isolates after detection
- [ ] Attach traces to JIRA ticket

Open questions / TODOs:
- Tune default thresholds per-model family (LLAMA-like vs transformers with long contexts).
- Add automated diff tooling that highlights top-3 kernel regressions between two full traces.
- Evaluate sampling rate tradeoffs at 0.1% vs 1% in large fleets.
- Consider integrating with observability alerts to auto-roll to fallback model on severe regressions.

Appendix: small example output (from local run, synthetic):
- config: N=64, mean-arrival=50ms, burst=200, mode=shared
- baseline p99: 220ms, current p99: 320ms (+45%)
- KV hit rate baseline: 87%, current: 69% (-18pp)
- top kernel delta: attention_kernel_v2 avg 8.4ms -> 11.7ms (+39%)
- preliminary hypothesis: eviction-induced KV miss spike caused extra compute + kernel warmup overhead; follow with dedicated replay and kernel microbench.
